title: The Matter of the Sacred Bull
body: There is a bull in Chhota Nagra that fears neither God nor the Penal Code. Sub-Inspector Diwan Chand petitions, with immense dignity, that this Brahminy beast has for the third time eaten the marigolds he grew for the flower show. ‘Let the bull be officially discouraged,’ he writes. ‘I ask no more.’

choices.label: Solemnly issue a written order that the bull be kept off official flowerbeds.
choices.outcome: The order is copied fair, framed, and hung in the police lines. The bull cannot read. Diwan Chand salutes it every morning, and honour is satisfied.

choices.label: Have the bull quietly relocated to a distant village.
choices.outcome: The bull goes by night in a commissariat cart. The receiving village takes a holy bull for an omen, and within the week a deputation arrives to ask what they have done to deserve it.

choices.label: Refuse to involve the district administration in bovine theology.
choices.outcome: Correct, dignified, useless. The marigolds are eaten a fourth time. Diwan Chand salutes you thereafter with a terrible punctilio, and never mentions flowers again.

title: The Billiards Subscription
body: Four annas on the billiards subscription, and the Chhota Nagra Club is convened in extraordinary session. Mrs. Fortescue-Vane is for. Major Prewitt is against, and says so twice. ‘It is the principle of the thing,’ says the Major, going purple. Both look to the new Magistrate to settle what has already ended two friendships.

choices.label: Side with Mrs. Fortescue-Vane. One does not cross her.
choices.outcome: You are now, invisibly and for ever, Mrs. Fortescue-Vane's man. In a station this size that is worth more than a knighthood, and she collects the interest at every dinner.

choices.label: Side with Major Prewitt and the principle of the thing.
choices.outcome: The Major wrings your hand as though you had relieved Mafeking. Mrs. Fortescue-Vane says nothing at all. You will learn what that silence costs by Christmas.

choices.label: Propose a sub-committee to study the matter.
choices.outcome: The sub-committee meets twice, quarrels once, and lapses. By the rains nobody remembers who was for and who against, and the billiards table wants new cloth in any case.

title: The Revenue Is Short
body: A telegram from Commissioner Blyth-Curram, who communicates in telegrams and disappointment: REVENUE RETURNS CHHOTA NAGRA UNSATISFACTORY STOP EXPECT IMPROVEMENT STOP NO EXCUSES REGARDING RAINFALL WILL BE ENTERTAINED STOP. The rains have failed. Every man in the district knows it except, officially, the Commissioner.

choices.label: Press the collection hard. Simla wants numbers.
choices.outcome: The returns improve, and the queue at Lala Hukum Chand's door lengthens with them. ‘The sahib's hukm,’ says the Lala, lending at his own rates. ‘Who am I to refuse?’

choices.label: Quietly grant remissions and massage the paperwork.
choices.outcome: Mercy off the books — the one sin the Service does not confess. The tahsildar enters the remissions in a hand rather smaller than usual and asks no questions. If Simla never looks, you are a sound officer. Simla mostly never looks.

choices.label: Send Simla a magnificent report explaining the rainfall.
choices.outcome: Blyth-Curram replies by return dak: RAINFALL NOTED STOP REVENUE STILL SHORT STOP. There is no third telegram.

title: The Tiger of Rampur
body: Villagers from Rampur report a tiger that has taken two goats and a good deal of sleep. They ask the Magistrate-sahib, as dastur demands, to come and shoot it. ‘The Collector before you shot three,’ says the headman, helpfully. You have fired a rifle four times in your life, twice by accident, and the district waits to learn whether the new sahib is a shikari or a clerk.

choices.label: Go out and shoot it yourself. It is expected.

ifTrue.outcome: Luck, and a range of eleven paces, and the tiger is down. Rampur skins him on the spot, and the tale is in three tehsils by Friday. Your hands do not stop shaking until dinner.

ifFalse.outcome: Your hand shakes and the shot goes wide into the khud. The tiger escapes; the story does not. In Rampur they are very polite about it, and that is worse than laughter.

choices.label: Send for a professional shikari from the next district.
choices.outcome: The shikari arrives with a Martini rifle and no conversation, and settles the matter in a night. Rampur is grateful, and faintly disappointed. The skin goes home with him.

choices.label: Declare it a matter for the Forest Department.
choices.outcome: Correct procedure. The Forest Department will attend to the tiger in the fullness of time, by which the tiger and everyone in Rampur understand: never.

title: The Rains Have Failed
body: There is no rain. There will be no rain, and the district knows what that means better than any word in the revenue code. Grain is up two seers to the rupee and climbing; the first families have sold their cooking-pots; a relief works could open to-morrow — if there were money, and Simla budgeted none.

choices.label: Open relief works at once and account for it later.
choices.outcome: Grain-for-labour on the roads and the Sonpur tank. They come in their thousands, thin but walking, and nobody starves. The treasury will want its accounting in April.

choices.label: Wait for sanction from Simla before spending a rupee.
choices.outcome: You wait, as the code directs. Sanction comes up by dak in six weeks — four weeks after the first deaths on the Rampur road. The file is faultless from first page to last.

choices.label: Lean on Lala Hukum Chand to release grain on credit.
choices.outcome: ‘For the sahib — anything,’ says Lala Hukum Chand, and names a rate that would make a Calcutta bank blush. The grain moves that night. The district will be paying for this famine long after it has forgotten the hunger.

title: The Commissioner Inspects
body: Commissioner Blyth-Curram descends upon Chhota Nagra in person, walrus-moustached and breathing grievance, to inspect the district, the treasury, the lock-up, and you. He will form his opinion in the first ten minutes and spend three days confirming it. The station has been whitewashed for the occasion — including, it is whispered, several things that were not walls.

choices.label: Show him a flawless, rehearsed district.
choices.outcome: Every ledger balances, every prisoner is suspiciously cheerful, and the road is mended along the one stretch he will drive. He leaves satisfied. The performance has cost you a fortnight and a small piece of your soul, and the Service counts that cheap.

choices.label: Show him the real district, warts and all.
choices.outcome: You show him the flooded quarter, the short revenue, the honest mess of the thing. He is appalled by your candour and, under the moustache, not altogether displeased. ‘You are frank, at any rate,’ he says at parting, and does not say it unkindly. None of it goes into the report.

choices.label: Ply him with the Club's best brandy and change the subject.
choices.outcome: By the second brandy he is telling you about his own first district; by the third the inspection is over, though neither of you says so. His report, when it comes, runs to two lines, both civil.

title: Fever in the Bazaar
body: Fever in the lanes behind the grain market — the Civil Surgeon says cholera; the bazaar says worse. ‘Cordon the quarter and close the wells to-day,’ says the Surgeon, ‘or count graves for me next week.’ The traders want the market open, the pilgrims want the road, and every man of them wants the choosing to be yours.

choices.label: Cordon the quarter and close the wells. Public health first.
choices.outcome: The fever is penned into forty houses and burns itself out there. The traders' memorial to Simla runs to nine pages, with signatures. The Surgeon says nothing, being busy.

choices.label: Keep the market open and hope the Surgeon is exaggerating.
choices.outcome: The market thrives for eleven days. On the twelfth the Surgeon is proved right in the way surgeons are proved right, and the cordon you refused at one street must now take in six.

choices.label: Split the difference: cordon quietly, keep up appearances.
choices.outcome: You do half of what the Surgeon asked and let each audience believe what suits it. The fever does rather less than its worst. The Surgeon, meeting you in the Mall thereafter, crosses the road.

title: A Question of Precedence
body: At the Club's cold-weather ball a dispute breaks out over precedence at dinner — whether the Executive Engineer's wife goes in before the Forest Officer's wife. A trifle, all agree; and a trifle of the kind that has poisoned stations from Peshawar to Madras for a full season together.

choices.label: Rule strictly by the Warrant of Precedence.
choices.outcome: You produce the actual Warrant of Precedence, an object roughly as sacred here as scripture, and settle the matter by the book. Both wives are furious — but at the book, which cannot be invited to dinner or snubbed at it.

choices.label: Seat them apart and pretend it was always so.
choices.outcome: A little fiction, gracefully served. The ball goes forward. You spend the cotillion by the dining-room door, sweating like a head waiter, and nobody thanks you.

choices.label: Declare you will not adjudicate the seating of a dinner.
choices.outcome: Principled, and a grave misreading of the station. Up-country, the seating of a dinner is the government. Both ladies now agree upon one point only, and the point is you.

title: The Case of the Stolen Buffalo
body: A cultivator stands charged with stealing his neighbour's buffalo. Nine witnesses swear one way, nine the other, and all eighteen are perjured. The truth — that the beast strayed and both men are lying about the rest — is not to be had in any shape the law can use. Both families watch your face for the verdict.

choices.label: Convict on the letter of the evidence.
choices.outcome: You convict the man the paper points at, who is guilty of something, if not of this. The law is satisfied. Justice was not called as a witness.

choices.label: Acquit for reasonable doubt and return the buffalo.
choices.outcome: Doubt to the accused, the buffalo to its likeliest owner, and a short homily to both families, who hear it with their eyes on the beast. They go out abusing each other and, mildly, you. The buffalo eats a court flowerbed on the way home.

choices.label: Bind both parties over and make them share the beast.
choices.outcome: Solomon in a solar topi. The two families are bound to joint custody of one bad-tempered buffalo, an arrangement so inconvenient to both that the shared grievance reconciles them within the year.

title: The Camp at Rampur
body: Your tents are pitched in the mango tope outside Rampur. Dung-smoke, a creaking well-wheel, the patwari’s cloth-bound registers on the camp table; and by sunrise a line of cultivators along the bund, come to lay their griefs before the sahib himself. This is the district as it is, and not as the files have it.

choices.label: Go through the land records line by line with the patwari.
choices.outcome: Three fields stand recorded to men who died in the last famine, and one to a man who never lived at all. ‘Clerical error,’ says the patwari, of each. By lamplight the register is truer than it was at noon.

choices.label: Hear the cultivators’ grievances under the mango tree.
choices.outcome: You sit till the lamps are lit, hearing of a bad well, a hard landlord, a boundary-stone that walks by night. You can mend perhaps one grief in five. The rest go home slower than they came, but they go home talking.

choices.label: Keep it brief — show the flag and move on.
choices.outcome: You are seen, saluted, and gone by noon. The tour diary records a village inspected. The village records that the sahib did not get down from his horse.

title: The River Comes Up
body: Three days of rain and the river is over its banks. The low villages are islands; the rail embankment is the only high ground for miles, and along it the flooded-out are gathering with their cattle and their cooking-pots. Boats are few, the light is going, and the water is still rising.

choices.label: Take personal charge of the rescue from a boat.
choices.outcome: Two nights on the water, hauling families off roof-trees by lantern-light, soaked through and of more use than you have felt in months. The district will tell for twenty years that the sahib came himself. You cough for a month.

choices.label: Organise from the embankment — relief camp, grain, order.
choices.outcome: You make the embankment a camp — grain, a rope-line, fires, a count kept of the living — and a frightened crowd does not become a mob. Nobody within reach of a boat is lost. Beyond the boats, the water keeps its own count.

choices.label: Wire for military help and hold the line till it comes.
choices.outcome: The sappers come up on the second day with pontoons and do the work handsomely. It was the sensible call. What the embankment saw was the sahib standing dry, waiting, and that is the picture that keeps.

title: The Procession and the Mosque
body: The great autumn procession of the one community goes, as it has gone a hundred years, down the lane past the other community’s chief mosque at the hour of prayer. Both parties are in your cutcherry by noon — the one pleading dastur, the other insult — and both have brought young men enough to show that the question is no longer the route.

choices.label: Order the procession to keep its ancient route.
choices.outcome: The procession passes under double police. A brick, some shoving, one lathi-charge that stops a yard short of a headline. Dastur is upheld. Next year is already forming in the lane.

choices.label: Divert the procession by a longer, quieter road.
choices.outcome: You turn it down the longer road in the name of peace. One side mutters that a hundred years of right is broken; the other says nothing, and puts the precedent away carefully, as a man puts away a knife. The year stays quiet.

choices.label: Summon both sides and broker a compromise yourself.
choices.outcome: Three days of tea, flattery, and threat in about equal parts, and there is a route, a timing, and a face-saving fiction apiece. It holds. No line of it will ever appear in any report.

title: The Dacoits of the Ravines
body: A gang has come up out of the ravine country — three villages robbed, a moneylender's house burned, and a growing suspicion among the cultivators that the sahib's writ stops where the metalled road does. The Superintendent wants a sweep; the villages want protection; the dacoits, by all accounts, want to become a legend.

choices.label: Lead an armed sweep of the ravines in person.
choices.outcome: A fortnight in the saddle in bad country, and the gang breaks — two taken, one shot, the rest over the border. The ravines go quiet. Within the month the ballad-singers have the story wrong, in your favour.

choices.label: Work quietly through informers and moneylenders.
choices.outcome: Money goes out in the dark and word comes back the same way. The gang is sold from inside by its own cook. There is no medal for this kind of work, and no report of it either.

choices.label: Post a reward and leave it to the police.
choices.outcome: The poster is much admired in three bazaars. The dacoits are not caught. In the ravine villages the doors go up an hour earlier at dusk, and nobody sends word of anything to anyone.

title: The District Budget
body: The annual estimates are due at the Secretariat, and the district's slender purse must be divided between what keeps people alive, what keeps people quiet, and what keeps Simla content. Ram Autar lays three drafts on the table, each balanced, each a small betrayal of the other two. ‘All are correct,’ he says, which is not the same as saying all are good.

choices.label: Fund public works — wells, roads, a dispensary.
choices.outcome: You spend on the unglamorous things a district actually needs. The wells get dug, the people are quietly better off, and the Secretariat notes that your establishment charges run above the provincial average. One of these facts will follow you. Guess which.

choices.label: Economise and return a surplus to the province.
choices.outcome: You send Simla a tidy surplus, and your district a leaking tank and a shut dispensary. The Financial Secretary writes that he is delighted. It is the only letter of praise you will get this year.

choices.label: Quietly strengthen the police lines.
choices.outcome: The money goes where it buys quiet rather than gratitude. The lock-up is mended, the constables paid on the first of the month, and the district grows a little safer and a little more watched. You tell yourself those are the same thing.

title: The Zamindar and the Tenants
body: The zamindar of Pipariya has raised his tenants' rents to a figure the land cannot bear, and the tenants — forty families, with the record on their side for once — have brought it to your court. The zamindar has brought his pleader, his account books, and a reminder, delivered smiling, that men of property are the natural friends of Government.

choices.label: Rule for the tenants and roll back the rents.
choices.outcome: You cut the rents to what the fields will yield. Forty families bless the sahib; the zamindar writes to the Commissioner on the dangerous radicalism of the young magistrate, and encloses, with regret, a list of his loyal services to the Crown.

choices.label: Rule for the zamindar — a contract is a contract.
choices.outcome: You uphold the letter of the lease. The revenue is secured, the men of property reassured, and forty families learn where they stand in the order of the sahib's cares. The Congress lecturer has their names within the month.

choices.label: Send it to arbitration and split the difference.
choices.outcome: The arbitrators find a rent that pinches all parties alike. Neither side thanks you, the record is muddied past appeal, and the reckoning goes over to some other magistrate in some other year.

title: A School for Sonpur
body: On tour you are met at Sonpur by villagers who have built a schoolhouse with their own hands and their own rupees, and ask of Government one thing only: a master and his pay. It is the self-help the annual report praises on one page, and the recurring charge the Finance Department strangles on the next.

choices.label: Sanction the master and the salary at once.
choices.outcome: You sign the sanction on the camp table, to the open astonishment of the deputation, who had budgeted a year of petitioning. ‘To-day, sahib?’ says the headman. ‘To-day.’ Sonpur gets its school, and you get the rarest pleasure the Service allows: a small good done quickly.

choices.label: Forward it through channels with a warm note.
choices.outcome: You do it properly, which is to say slowly. The file begins its long pilgrimage through the Education Department. The schoolhouse waits, swept and empty, a small monument to the distance between a village and the Secretariat.

choices.label: Praise their spirit and make no promises.
choices.outcome: You give them a handsome speech on self-reliance, and no master with it. The schoolhouse stands swept and empty through the rains, and the children go back to minding goats.

title: The Boycott of Foreign Cloth
body: They are burning Manchester cloth in the bazaar — the swadeshi men, singing while it burns — and the mill-agents and box-wallahs, loyal men and taxpayers all, demand that you put a stop to this seditious destruction of perfectly good imported goods. The cloth, inconveniently, is the burners' own property.

choices.label: Ban the bonfires as a breach of the peace.
choices.outcome: You forbid the burnings, and thereby proclaim that Government fears the loss of a man's own shirt. The box-wallahs send round their thanks and a case of whisky. The Congress paper prints your order in full, without one word of comment.

choices.label: Permit it — a man may burn his own cloth.
choices.outcome: You decline to defend Manchester from the citizens of Chhota Nagra. The bonfires burn out in a week, as bonfires do, and the mill-agents write to the Chamber of Commerce about the alarming sympathies of the local magistrate.

choices.label: Look the other way and buy some khadi yourself.
choices.outcome: You have a coat of homespun quietly made up and wear it on tour. It is comfortable, and it is a small treason. Ram Autar looks at it once, and looks away, and is silent for the length of the morning.

title: A Scandal at the Club
body: In the dead of the hot weather, with tempers and thermometers both past bearing, young Pemberton of the Police has been discovered in a compromising arrangement involving another man's wife, a great deal of the Club's whisky, and a challenge shouted across the billiard-room. As senior civil officer present, you inherit the mess entire.

choices.label: Hush it up and send Pemberton on sudden leave.
choices.outcome: A transfer on medical certificate, a story about his liver, and the station agrees, as stations do, to have seen nothing. Pemberton is gone by Thursday's train. His bar chits are settled anonymously.

choices.label: Report it properly up the chain.
choices.outcome: You do the honest thing and put it on paper. Pemberton is broken; the wronged husband is not comforted; and the station marks you down as a man who cannot keep a thing quiet. At a small mess there is no blacker mark.

choices.label: Bang heads together and settle it over brandy.
choices.outcome: You lock the three of them in the card-room with a decanter and stand at the door until there is an apology, a handshake, and a common understanding that the alternative is you. It answers. Your faith in the ruling race does not come out of that room with them.

title: The Commissioner's Durbar
body: A grand durbar is to be held — the Commissioner presiding, the district's notables ranked on the maidan, robes of honour given out, loyalty affirmed, the whole theatre of the Raj staged for an afternoon. Yours is the seating. A chair an inch too low, a name called out of turn, and a feud is born that will outlive you and your successor both.

choices.label: Stage it flawlessly by the Warrant and the old lists.
choices.outcome: Every notable is seated to the inch of his izzat, every robe bestowed on cue, and the durbar goes like clockwork wound by a nervous man. The Commissioner is pleased; the notables are placated; you have spent a week of your life on a seating plan and would, appallingly, do it again.

choices.label: Use the seating to reward the loyal, cool the awkward.
choices.outcome: You move the friends of Government quietly up the rows and let the difficult men feel the draught at the back. It is deftly done and widely understood: an afternoon of pageantry made into a small sharp instrument. The Pandit, who was not invited, is said to have laughed.

choices.label: Keep it plain and spend the saving on the district.
choices.outcome: You stage a modest durbar and put the difference into a relief fund. The notables are faintly insulted to be honoured on a budget; the district notices that the sahib would rather feed it than flatter it. Only one of those parties writes the confidential reports.
